blocks.text: It is proved from the Arabic language that רחם racham is a species of vulture.

Now, given the hesitation of the interpreters that we have described, who would deny that it is safest to consult the Arabs? For the bird رخم [rakham] racham, or رخمة [rakhama] rachama, is very well known among them even today, and it is described by many, as what follows will make plain. Damir: الرخمة طاير ابقع يشبه النسر في الخلقة [al-rakhama ṭāyir abqaʿ yushbih al-nasr fī al-khilqa] Rachama, a bird of variegated colour, approaching the nature of the eagle. And a little later: وفي طبع هذا الطاير انه لا يرضي من الجبال الا من بالوحش منها ولا من الاماكن الا بالاسحقها والابعدها من اماكن اعداية ولا من الهضاب الا بصخورها ويقال لها لانوق [wa-fī ṭabʿ hādhā al-ṭāyir annahu lā yarḍī min al-jibāl illā min bi-l-waḥsh minhā wa-lā min al-amākin illā bi-l-asḥaqihā wa-l-abʿadihā min amākin aʿdāyih wa-lā min al-hiḍāb illā bi-ṣukhūrihā wa-yuqāl lahā lānūq] It is the nature of this bird that it does not like mountains unless they are extremely solitary; nor other places, unless they are very far apart and most remote from inhabited places; and among rocky places only inaccessible crags. It is called by another name anuk. And below: وتبيض بيضة واحدة وربما اتامت وهي من ليام الطير وهن ثلاث الغراب والبوم والرخم والعرب تضرب المثل في الامتناع ببيضها فيقولون اعز من بيض الانوق وابعد من بيض الانوق فانه لا يكاد [col. 304] يظفر به لان اوكارها في روس الجبال والاماكن الصعبة كما تقدم قال الشاعر ۞ [wa-tabīḍ bayḍa wāḥida wa-rubbamā atāmat wa-hiya min liyām al-ṭayr wa-hunna thalāth al-ghurāb wa-l-būm wa-l-rakham wa-l-ʿarab taḍrib al-mathal fī al-imtināʿ bi-bayḍihā fa-yaqūlūn aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq wa-abʿad min bayḍ al-anūq fa-innahu lā yakād yuẓfar bihi li-anna awkārahā fī rūs al-jibāl wa-l-amākin al-ṣaʿba kamā taqaddam qāla al-shāʿir]
وكنت اذا استودعت سر ۞ اكتمت كبيض انوق لا ينال لها وكر ۞ [wa-kuntu idhā istawdaʿtu sirr aktamtu ka-bayḍ anūq lā yunāl lahā wakr]

And it lays a single egg, but sometimes it also produces twins. It is one of the birds called liam (as if you were to say ignoble). These are three: the raven, the little owl and the racham. There is a proverb among the Arabs signifying how inaccessible its eggs are: “Rarer than the egg of the anuk”, or “More remote than the egg of the anuk”: for hardly anyone reaches it, because it nests on the summit of mountains and in precipitous places, as was said before. Hence the poet said: “And when I was called apart into a hidden place, I was concealed like the egg of the anuk, whose nest is inaccessible”. Alkazuinius: رخمه طاير النسر في خلقته يختار لبيضه اطراف الجبال [III, 57] الشاهقة ليصعب الوصول الي بيضه يقال اعز من بيض الانوق فاذا جاء اوان بيضها ذهبت الي الهند واتت حجر يقال له ابوطاقيون وهو حجر مدور مثل خرزة اذا حركت تعقعق في جوفه حجر اخر ويترك ذلك الحجر تحتها فتبيض من غير وجع وتطير خلف العساكر لتاكل من جيف [rakhama ṭāyir al-nasr fī khilqatih yakhtār li-bayḍih aṭrāf al-jibāl al-shāhiqa li-yaṣʿub al-wuṣūl ilā bayḍih yuqāl aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq fa-idhā jāʾa awān bayḍihā dhahabat ilā al-hind wa-atat ḥajar yuqāl lahu abūṭāqiyūn wa-huwa ḥajar mudawwar mithl kharaza idhā ḥurrikat taʿaqʿaqa fī jawfih ḥajar ākhar wa-yutrak dhālika al-ḥajar taḥtahā fa-tabīḍ min ghayr wajaʿ wa-taṭīr khalf al-ʿasākir li-taʾkul min jiyaf] Rachama is an eagle bird (that is, of the aquiline kind). It is its nature to choose the summits of the highest mountains for its eggs, so that access to them may be more difficult. Hence the saying, “Rarer than the egg of the anuk” (that is, of the rachama). When it is about to lay its eggs, it goes to India and brings from there a stone which they call abutacium (rather, εὐτόκιον [eutokion]). This stone is round like a pearl. When it is moved, another stone sounds inside it. With this stone placed under itself, it lays its eggs without pain. It follows armies in its flight, to feed on the corpses of the slain. Alcamus: الانوق العقاب الرخمة وطاير اسود له كالعرف او اسود اصلع الراس اصفر المنقار وهو اعز من بيض الانوق لانها تحرزها فلا يكاد يظفر به لان اوكارها في التلل الصعبة قيل [col. 305] فاخلاقها عشر خصال تحصن بيضها وتحمي فرجها وتالف ولدها ولا تمكن من نفسها غير زوجها وتقطع في اول القواطع وترجع في اول الرواجع وتطير في التحسير ولا تغتر بالشكير ولا ترب بالوكور ولا تسقط علي الجفر بالشكير [al-anūq al-ʿuqāb al-rakhama wa-ṭāyir aswad lahu ka-l-ʿurf aw aswad aṣlaʿ al-raʾs aṣfar al-minqār wa-huwa aʿazz min bayḍ al-anūq li-annahā taḥruzuhā fa-lā yakād yuẓfar bihi li-anna awkārahā fī al-tilal al-ṣaʿba qīla fa-akhlāquhā ʿashar khiṣāl tuḥaṣṣin bayḍahā wa-taḥmī farkhahā wa-taʾlaf waladahā wa-lā tumakkin min nafsihā ghayr zawjihā wa-taqṭaʿ fī awwal al-qawāṭiʿ wa-tarjiʿ fī awwal al-rawājiʿ wa-taṭīr fī al-taḥsīr wa-lā taghtarr bi-l-shakīr wa-lā tarubb bi-l-wukūr wa-lā tasquṭ ʿalā al-jafr bi-l-shakīr] Anuk, a kind of eagle, which is also called rachama. A black bird, which has something like a mane. Others say: a black bird with a bald head and a yellow beak, about which there is the proverb, “Rarer than the egg of the anuk”; because it guards its egg so well that it can hardly be attacked. For it nests in inaccessible mountains. Ten peculiarities are attributed to it. 1. It protects its eggs. 2. It guards its young. 3. It always stays close to its offspring. 4. It does nothing on its own without its mate. 5. It migrates with the first migrants. 6. It returns with the first to return. 7. It flies during the moulting of its feathers. 8. Nor is it endangered by the scantiness of its feathers. 9. Nor does it remain in the nest. 10. Nor does it fall into an inability to mate: as the other birds do when their feathers have fallen out. Of these ten peculiarities the first four are also found in Damir, in almost the same words. Andreas Bellunensis: Alrachame is a large bird like a kite, with white body plumage and black wing feathers. It eats putrid flesh and the like. In [III, 58] Syria it is abundant ^{(1)}. On the Sura of the Qur'an الاخراب [al-akhrāb] Alachrab, which in the Latin translator is Azoara 43, where Moses is treated, towards the end, the Commentator Abulabas Cordubensis says: لم يعرف موضع قبره الا الرخم فلذلك جعله الله اصم ابكم [lam yaʿrif mawḍiʿ qabrih illā al-rakham fa-li-dhālika jaʿalahu allāh aṣamm abkam] No one knew the place of his tomb except the bird racham, and therefore God made it deaf and dumb. This is entirely fabulous, like most things of such triflers. For, to say nothing of the rest, this bird is extremely vocal, like the whole aquiline and vulturine kind. Accordingly, as the Arabs often attribute any words they like to birds, as we do to bells, Zamachsari writes that the cry of the rachama sounds roughly like these words: سبحان ربي الاعلي [subḥān rabbī al-aʿlī] Sobchan rabbi alali, that is, Praise to my Lord most high.
